name: Activated charcoal cleanse

lead: Activated charcoal is a highly porous carbon that adsorbs many substances in the digestive tract. A cleanse applies it as a wellness routine, with proponents expecting less bloating, a flatter stomach and clearer skin.

In medicine, activated charcoal is used for oral poisonings and overdoses and is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines.[2] Its use as a general detox has not been shown in published studies to improve the body's own elimination, according to a reference summary of the topic; short-term trials have looked at gas relief and cholesterol.[1]

paras: Cleanses are described as a course of charcoal capsules or powder taken for a few days, sometimes in juices or charcoal-coloured foods and drinks, within wellness routines. Forum users discuss it alongside other gut-focused routines such as apple cider vinegar or psyllium cleanses.

Charcoal is non-selective, so it can bind medications and nutrients; sources advise people on medications such as birth control pills and antidepressants to avoid charcoal-coloured novelty products.[2] Reported effects include constipation, vomiting and black stools, and aspiration into the lungs can be dangerous.[1][2]

angle.text: Users take it hoping for a flatter stomach and clearer skin. The pathway is claimed rather than established in trials.

lead: An activated charcoal cleanse is a wellness regimen in which people take activated charcoal by mouth in the hope of removing toxins from the gut. Proponents link it to less bloating, clearer skin and weight loss, which is where its appearance appeal comes from.[1]

Activated carbon is made by heating carbon-rich material such as wood or coconut shell and then activating it to create an enormous internal surface area, which lets it bind molecules by physical adsorption.[1] In clinics it is used soon after ingestion of certain poisons, and it is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines.[2]

Its binding is non-selective, so it also takes up medicines and nutrients, and it is ineffective against several substances including alcohols, lithium and iron.[1][2] A food trend in 2016 put charcoal into items such as ice cream and bagels.[2]

paras: The regimen is a short course of oral charcoal meant to cleanse the gut. Grokipedia's summary describes claims of reduced bloating, clearer skin and weight loss in alternative-health contexts.[1]

Activated charcoal works by physisorption: molecules cling to its porous surface through weak forces, and effectiveness is highest soon after ingestion, ideally within about an hour.[1] It binds poorly to small or polar molecules such as alcohols, lithium, and iron.[1][2]

Charcoal has been used medicinally since antiquity, with Egyptian papyri from about 1500 BC reportedly describing its use on wounds and intestinal complaints, according to Grokipedia.[1] A charcoal food trend appeared in 2016.[2]

Reviews summarised in Grokipedia report that no peer-reviewed study has shown that a general charcoal cleanse enhances liver or kidney elimination, and mention limited short-term findings on cholesterol and gas.[1] Wikipedia states that over-the-counter charcoal has no effect on intestinal gas or diarrhea.[2] Proponents' reports of reduced bloating are anecdotal.

Reported adverse effects include constipation, vomiting and black stools, with interference with nutrient and drug absorption.[1] Wikipedia notes that people taking contraceptives or antidepressants are advised to avoid charcoal-coloured novelty foods because it may make their medication ineffective, and that aspiration can be fatal.[2]
No studies found. Charcoal has been studied for poisoning treatment, which is a different use from a cleanse.[1]

lore.intro: Charcoal cleanses come up in training-forum threads about gut and bloating routines, usually next to other cleanse products.

claims.claim: A charcoal cleanse removes toxins and reduces bloating
Charcoal is harmless because it is not absorbed
